463.title: Pranayama (2.49–2.53)
463.hook: with the seat settled, the breath is next, and Patanjali says it thins the covering over the mind's light
463.tomorrow: Pratyahara — the senses follow the mind home
463.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice pranayama as part of daily worship, for instance before reciting the Gayatri mantra in the morning, and yoga teachers usually introduce breath retention gradually and under supervision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asana, a seat, steady and comfortable, and your line, that's all it says. Did you check a chair today for steady and easy? Day four hundred sixty-three.

You step out of a hot shower and the bathroom mirror is solid white. You can't see a thing. You could scrub it with a towel and leave streaks. Or you could open the door a crack, let the air move, and wait. Slowly, from the edges in, the fog lifts, and there you are. You didn't put your face back in the mirror. It was there the whole time. Patanjali's fourth limb works on the breath, and the reason he gives for it sounds a lot like that mirror.
screen: `A FOGGED MIRROR.` → `DON'T SCRUB. LET THE AIR MOVE.` → `IT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Prana is life breath, the energy that moves in breathing. The second part of the word is read two ways: ayama, stretching out, or yama, reining in. Teachers have used both, and both fit. Sutra 2.49 begins: once the seat is settled, pranayama is the pausing of the flow of in-breath and out-breath. Then 2.50 describes it. The breath can be outer, inner, or held still, and it's measured by place, time and number. And it becomes, in his words, long and subtle. Not forceful. Not heroic. Long and fine, like thread. Sutra 2.51 adds a fourth kind, one that goes beyond outer and inner, where the breath seems to settle on its own. Then the reason, in 2.52: from this, the covering over the light thins away. The light is the mind's clarity. It was never missing. It was covered. The classical commentary says the covering is the karma that hides discernment, and it repeats an old saying: there is no discipline higher than pranayama. It burns away impurity and lets the light of knowledge shine. Finally 2.53: and the mind becomes fit for concentration. Pranayama isn't the destination. It's what gets the mind ready for the inner limbs. A practical note: strong breath-holding is something people learn in person, with a teacher, and none of it is needed here. What anyone can do is what 2.50 points to. Let the breath get a little longer, a little finer, and watch the fog lift on its own.
screen: `PRANA: THE LIFE BREATH.` · `LONG AND SUBTLE.` · `THE COVERING OVER THE LIGHT THINS.` · `THE MIND GROWS FIT TO FOCUS.` · then, large: `THE VEIL THINS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice makes the breath long and subtle, gently. Sit steady and easy. Let a few breaths go by as they are. Then let each out-breath be a little longer than the in-breath, with no strain and no holding. Make the breath quieter, so quiet you could barely hear it yourself. If you feel short of air at any point, go back to normal breathing. Then simply watch the mind, and notice whether anything clears. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama. Working with the life breath, letting it grow long and subtle, the fourth limb of yoga.
Your line: the veil thins. Today, when your mind fogs up, in traffic, in a meeting, take three long, quiet out-breaths and let it clear from the edges in. Day four hundred sixty-three.

464.title: Pratyahara — the senses follow the mind home (2.54–2.55)
464.hook: the fifth limb: when the mind settles, the senses settle with it, like bees following their leader home
464.howItsDone: In yoga practice, pratyahara is usually cultivated by resting attention on one object, such as the breath or a mantra, until the senses quiet; teachers often cite the Gita's tortoise drawing in its limbs as the classic image.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pranayama, the breath grown long and subtle, and your line, the veil thins. Did three long out-breaths clear the fog somewhere today? Day four hundred sixty-four.

Try to stop hearing the fridge hum. Really try. Clench, focus, tell your ears to quit. It gets louder. Now remember the last time you were lost in a great book or a deep conversation. The fridge was humming then too. You didn't hear it. Nobody told your ears to stop. Your attention went somewhere, and your ears simply followed it. Today is the last limb of the outer five, and the last sutras of book two. Patanjali's answer to the noisy senses isn't to fight them. It's to move the mind, and let the senses follow.
screen: `TRY NOT TO HEAR THE FRIDGE.` → `IT GETS LOUDER.` → `LOST IN A BOOK, IT'S GONE.`

segments.voice: Prati means back, toward. Ahara means taking in, even food. Pratyahara: drawing back, withdrawal. Sutra 2.54 describes it: when the senses aren't joined to their objects, they take on, as it were, the nature of the mind itself. The classical commentary gives the picture. A swarm of bees follows its leader, which the commentary calls the king of the bees. When the leader flies up, they all fly up. When it settles, they all settle. So with the senses and the mind. Restrain the mind, and the senses come home on their own. You don't chase each bee. Sutra 2.55: from this, supreme mastery of the senses. The commentary lists other views of what mastering the senses might mean, enjoying only what's allowed, or using them without being hooked, and then says the highest is this: when the mind is one-pointed, the senses don't go out at all. The Bhagavad Gita has a neighbor image, the tortoise drawing its limbs into its shell. And notice where pratyahara sits. It's the hinge of the eight. The first five limbs face outward: others, yourself, body, breath, senses. The last three face inward. Which also means book two ends here. Look at the road it's walked: kriya yoga, discipline, study, surrender. The five afflictions, from not seeing to the fear of death. Karma's storehouse. Suffering, and its cause, and its cure, discernment. Then the outer limbs, one by one. All of it, a way of calling the bees home.
screen: `PRATI-AHARA: DRAWING BACK.` · `THE BEES FOLLOW THEIR LEADER.` · `MIND SETTLES, SENSES SETTLE.` · `THE HINGE OF THE EIGHT LIMBS.` · then, large: `WITHDRAWAL.`

segments.voice: Today's practice calls the bees home. Sit steady and easy. Let the breath be long and quiet. Now give the mind one place to rest, the feeling of the breath at the tip of the nose. Don't try to block sounds or sights. Just keep going back to that one place. Every time a noise pulls you, don't fight it, return to the breath, and notice whether the hearing quiets a little on its own, following the mind. The bell holds the time.
Pratyahara. The drawing back of the senses, the fifth limb: when the mind settles, the senses follow it home.

Your line: withdrawal. Today, when something noisy keeps pulling at you, a phone, a screen, a sound, don't fight it. Give your mind one better place to go, and let the senses follow. Day four hundred sixty-four.

465.title: Concentration, meditation, absorption (3.1–3.3)
465.hook: book three opens with the three inner limbs in three short sutras: hold the mind in one place, let it flow, then disappear into what you're seeing
465.howItsDone: In Hindu meditation traditions, practitioners often fix attention on a point such as the heart, the space between the eyebrows, a sacred image or a mantra, and teachers describe concentration deepening into meditation and absorption over long practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pratyahara, and your line, withdrawal. The senses follow the mind home, like bees following their leader. That closed book two. Today, book three opens. Day four hundred sixty-five.

There's a story often told from the Mahabharata. The teacher Drona sets a wooden bird high in a tree and calls his students to aim at its eye. Before each one shoots, he asks: what do you see? One sees the tree, the branches, the sky, his brothers. Drona sends him away. Then Arjuna steps up. What do you see? The bird. Describe the bird. I see only its head. Shoot. Popular retellings make it the eye; the epic says the head. Book three of the Yoga Sutras is called Vibhuti, the book of powers. But it opens with Arjuna's kind of seeing, in three steps.
screen: `A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `ONLY ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.1: dharana, concentration, is binding the mind to one place. The classical commentary lists places: the navel, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, or something outside the body. Dharana comes from a root meaning to hold, the same root as dharma. You hold the mind there, the way you'd hold a cup steady. Of course it slips. You bring it back. That's dharana. Sutra 3.2: dhyana, meditation, is when the idea of that object flows on without a break. One thread, no knots. A later image some teachers use: oil poured from one jar to another, a single unbroken stream. Not holding anymore. Flowing. Sutra 3.3: samadhi, absorption, is that same flow when only the object shines, as if empty of its own form. Here the sutra is precise. In dhyana, there's still you, meditating on something. In samadhi, the sense of me meditating drops away. Only the bird's head. Arjuna in the story isn't thinking, I'm concentrating well. There's just the target. Three sutras, three words, and they're not three separate techniques. They're one movement, deepening. Hold. Flow. Disappear into it. There's a small, everyday version: being so absorbed in a song, a game, a sick child's breathing, that the self drops out of view. Patanjali's claim is that this can be trained, and pointed at the deepest things.
screen: `DHARANA: HOLD THE MIND IN ONE PLACE.` · `DHYANA: AN UNBROKEN FLOW.` · `SAMADHI: ONLY THE OBJECT SHINES.` · `ONE MOVEMENT, DEEPENING.` · then, large: `DHARANA, DHYANA, SAMADHI.`

segments.voice: Today's practice tries the first step, and maybe the second. Sit steady and easy. Choose one place, the tip of the nose where the breath touches, or the center of the chest. Hold the mind there. When it slips, and it will, bring it back without scolding. That's dharana. If, for a few breaths, it stays without your holding, notice the flow. That's a taste of dhyana. Whatever happens, keep returning. The bell holds the time.
Concentration. Dharana, binding the mind to one place, the first of the three inner limbs, which deepen into meditation and absorption.

Your line: dharana, dhyana, samadhi. Today, do one ordinary task, washing a cup, signing a form, with only that in view. Hold, flow, and see if you disappear into it for a moment. Day four hundred sixty-five.

466.title: The three together (3.4–3.8)
466.hook: concentration, meditation and absorption on one object get a single name, samyama, the tool the rest of book three is built on
466.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras present samyama as the combined practice of the three inner limbs on a single object, learned gradually over years, and they stress that its insights are steps toward liberation rather than the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: concentration, then meditation, then absorption. Hold, flow, disappear into it. Did one ordinary task get your whole attention for a moment? Day four hundred sixty-six.

Watch someone braid hair. Three strands, each one loose and floppy on its own. Left over middle. Right over middle. Again, again. And somewhere along the way, three strands stop being three strands. They become one braid, strong enough to hold its shape all day. Nobody would call it three things anymore. Yesterday Patanjali gave three inner limbs: concentration, meditation, absorption. Today he braids them. And the braid gets its own name, a name that will carry the rest of book three.

Sutra 3.4: the three together are samyama. Sam means together. Yama you already know, from the first limb: reining in, holding. Samyama, holding together. Concentration, meditation and absorption, all on the same object, at once. From here on, whenever Patanjali says, by samyama on this, that happens, this is the tool he means. Sutra 3.5: by mastering it, the light of insight. Prajna, wisdom, begins to shine. Sutra 3.6: it's applied in stages. You don't jump to the top. The classical commentary adds a striking line here: yoga is to be known by yoga, and yoga grows out of yoga. In other words, each stage, practiced, opens the next. Then two sutras about inside and outside. Sutra 3.7: these three are inner, compared with the five limbs before. The restraints, the observances, the seat, the breath, the senses drawing back: those are the outer limbs. Concentration, meditation, absorption: the inner ones. And then 3.8, the humbling line: even these are outer, compared with the seedless. Remember seedless samadhi, from the end of book one? Absorption with no object at all, no seed left to sprout. Measured against that, even the braid is still on the outside. So samyama is powerful, and Patanjali is about to spend most of a book on what it can do. But he's told you up front: it isn't the end of the road.
screen: `SAMYAMA: HOLDING TOGETHER.` · `MASTERED, INSIGHT SHINES.` · `YOGA IS KNOWN BY YOGA.` · `EVEN THESE ARE OUTER TO THE SEEDLESS.` · then, large: `SAMYAMA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice braids the three on something simple. Sit steady and easy, and choose one object: the breath at the nose, or a single sound. Hold the mind there, concentration. Let the holding become a flow, meditation. If for a moment there's only the breath and no one doing the breathing, let that be. Often the mind stays on the first strand, and that's the work. Keep braiding. The bell holds the time.
Prajna, wisdom's light, which begins to shine when samyama is mastered: concentration, meditation and absorption held on one object at once, the tool of book three.
Your line: samyama. Today, pick one thing to study with all three strands for one full minute: a leaf, a face, a sentence. See what it shows you. Day four hundred sixty-six.

467.title: The transformations of mind (3.9–3.15)
467.hook: even stillness is a kind of change, and the same mark can mean one, ten or a hundred depending on where it stands
467.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras study the transformations of 3.9–3.15 with the classical commentary, and in meditation practitioners watch thoughts arise and fade as a way of seeing change clearly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prajna, and your line, samyama. Concentration, meditation and absorption, braided on one thing. What did one full minute of looking show you? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

Write the number one on a piece of paper. A single upright stroke. Now put a zero after it. Same stroke, same ink, same paper, and it means ten. Add another zero. A hundred. The stroke didn't grow. Nothing about it changed, and yet everything about what it means changed, just by where it stands. The classical commentary on the Yoga Sutras uses this very example: one mark, worth one, ten or a hundred by its place. It's explaining today's sutras, about how things change, including the mind.
screen: `ONE STROKE OF A PEN.` → `ONE, TEN, A HUNDRED.` → `THE STROKE NEVER CHANGED.`

segments.voice: The word is parinama: transformation, change of form. Patanjali starts with the mind. Sutra 3.9: even stillness is a change. There's a moment when a scattering impression fades and a stilling impression rises, and the mind shifts toward quiet. Sutra 3.10: practiced again and again, that shift becomes a calm, steady flow. Then 3.11: scatteredness wanes, one-pointedness rises. And 3.12: the thought that fades and the thought that rises become alike, the same object, moment after moment. That's one-pointedness, described as a kind of change. Then he widens the lens. Sutra 3.13 says the same three changes run through everything, the elements and the senses too: change of property, change of time, change of condition. The commentary gives the stroke of the pen, and another picture: the same woman is called mother, daughter and sister, depending on who's speaking. Sutra 3.14 names what stays underneath: the substance that carries the properties, past, present and still to come. And 3.15: a different order produces a different change. The commentary's example is clay. A lump becomes a pot. The pot breaks into shards. The shards become dust. The clay is there the whole way through. Why put this in a book on meditation? Because if you're going to do samyama on anything, you need to see clearly what changes and what carries the change. And in the Yoga Sutras' wider picture, the seer itself doesn't change at all. Only the seen does.

segments.voice: Today's practice watches change happen in the mind. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Notice a thought arise, stay a moment and fade. Notice the next. Don't follow the stories. Just watch the shape: rising, staying, fading. Then notice the breath, also rising and fading. And notice what doesn't seem to rise and fade: the watching itself. Stay with that for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Parinama, change of form. Even stillness and one-pointedness are changes, carried by something that stays.
Your line: what changes. Today, notice one thing changing, coffee cooling, light moving across a wall, your own mood, and ask what's carrying the change. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

468.title: Knowledge of past and future (3.16)
468.hook: the first of the powers in book three follows straight from yesterday: see how a thing changes, all the way, and you see where it came from and where it's going
468.howItsDone: The siddhis of Yoga Sutras book three are studied in yoga lineages as signs of mastery; Hindu stories describe sages who know past and future, and teachers often caution students not to make such powers their goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parinama, and your line, what changes. Lump, pot, shards, and the clay all the way through. What did you catch changing? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

A forester cuts a slice from a fallen oak and counts the rings. This thin one, a dry year. This dark scar, a fire. These wide ones, good rain. She can read a century of weather in a circle of wood. And if you ask her, she can tell you something about the years ahead too: how this stand of trees will grow, which ones will need light. She isn't psychic. She just understands, deeply, how wood changes. Today the powers of book three begin, and the first one sounds like her.
screen: `A SLICE OF OAK.` → `A DRY YEAR, A FIRE, GOOD RAIN.` → `THE POWERS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.16: by samyama on the three transformations, knowledge of the past and the future. Remember the three from yesterday: change of property, change of time, change of condition. The lump becoming the pot. The future pot hidden in the clay, the past lump still in the pot. Patanjali's claim follows from that. If concentration, meditation and absorption rest fully on how a thing changes, the whole arc opens up: where it's been, where it's heading. The word for past is atita, what has gone by. Future is anagata, what has not yet come. You heard anagata a couple of weeks ago, in the pain not yet come, to be avoided. The word for these powers in general is siddhi, an accomplishment, a perfection, and this is the first of a long list. Over the next days Patanjali will name many: knowing other minds, strength, the inner map of the body, and stranger things. How are they meant? The classical commentators take them as real capacities that come with deep practice, and the stories of sages tell of them. Some readers take them more inwardly, as pictures of what clear seeing makes possible. The sutras themselves list them plainly, without bragging, and before the list is done they'll add a warning, which we'll hear in its place. For now, notice how ordinary the first power's logic is. It isn't magic fire. It's the forester's eye, taken all the way. Understanding change so completely that time opens in both directions.

segments.voice: Today's practice reads one small arc. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Then bring to mind one object near you, a mug, a plant, your own hand. Ask quietly: where did this come from? Clay, a seed, your parents. Where is it going? Shards, compost, age. No need for answers you can't know. Just let the object open in both directions, past and future, and then come back to the breath, which is only now. The bell holds the time.
Siddhi, an accomplishment, a perfection. The first of the powers in book three, from samyama on how a thing changes.
Your line: the powers begin. Today, look at one thing the way the forester reads wood: what made it this way, and what will it become? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

469.title: Knowledge of others' minds (3.19)
469.hook: samyama on another person's state of mind reveals that mind, and the very next sutra draws a line around what it can't see
469.howItsDone: Many Hindu stories describe sages who know the minds of those who come to them, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras point to 3.20's limit and to the yamas as the frame in which any such power is held.

segments.voice: Yesterday: siddhi, and your line, the powers begin. See how a thing changes, all the way, and time opens both ways. Day four hundred sixty-nine, the end of a week.

Your phone buzzes. It's your oldest friend. One word: hey. No punctuation. And somehow you already know something's wrong. Not what. Just that. You've read a thousand of their heys, and this one is different. You text back: what happened? Nobody calls that a superpower. It's what close attention to one person, for years, starts to do. Today Patanjali names a power that sounds like a much bigger version of that. And then, immediately, he tells you exactly where it stops.
screen: `ONE WORD: HEY.` → `SOMETHING'S WRONG.` → `NOT WHAT. JUST THAT.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.19: by samyama on the idea in another's mind, knowledge of that other mind. The word is pratyaya, the content of awareness at a given moment, the mood or idea running through it. Rest concentration, meditation and absorption on that, and the other person's state of mind becomes clear: troubled, calm, grasping, glad. Then comes the warning, in the very next line. Sutra 3.20: but not its object. You can know that the mind is angry, but not what it's angry at, because that wasn't the object of the samyama. The classical commentary is careful here. The power reaches the color of the mind, not its whole story. That's honest, and a little humbling. Even at its height, knowing another person has a limit, and the sutra writes the limit right into the power. It's worth sitting with the order of the book, too. Patanjali didn't open with powers. He opened with non-harm, truth, not stealing. Anyone who reads a mind is standing very close to someone else's inner life, and the first limb has already said how to stand there. Now the week, looked at from the top. Pranayama, the veil thins. Pratyahara, the senses follow the mind home. Concentration, meditation, absorption. Prajna, samyama. The transformations, what changes. Past and future. And today, other minds, with a line drawn around them. A week that went inward, and now begins to turn outward again, toward what that inward work can do.
screen: `PRATYAYA: WHAT'S IN A MIND NOW.` · `KNOW THE MIND, NOT ITS OBJECT.` · `THE LIMIT IS WRITTEN IN.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `AND THE WARNING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice reads the closest mind there is, your own. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Then ask: what's the color of my mind right now? Restless, tired, glad, worried. Name it in one word. Don't chase the reasons behind it. Just the color. Breathe with it. Then, if you like, bring to mind someone you love, and wish their mind well, whatever color it is today. The bell holds the time.
Pratyaya, the mood or idea running through someone's awareness. By samyama on another's state of mind, that mind is known, though not what it's fixed on.
Your line: and the warning. Today, when you sense someone's mood, let that be enough. Ask, don't assume the reason. Day four hundred sixty-nine.
